questions.question: Why is String immutable in Java?
questions.title: Why Is String Immutable in Java?
questions.direct_answer: A `String` in Java is immutable because its internal character array is `private final`, the class itself is `final`, and no method in the class ever modifies the stored characters. Once created, the content of a String can never change — operations like `concat()` or `toUpperCase()` always return a new String object, leaving the original untouched.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know what immutability means in practice, the three design choices that enforce it, and the real benefits it provides — not just the textbook definition.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'String variables can't be changed' — that's wrong. The variable can be reassigned (`s = s + '!')`) but the original String object itself is unchanged. A new object is created.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give concrete benefits: thread safety (no synchronization needed), String pool (same literal can be safely shared), security (class loader can't be tricked by a mutated class name), and HashMap key reliability (hashCode never changes).

sections.title: The Object Is Frozen — Only the Variable Can Move
sections.content:
An **immutable** object is one whose value can never change after it is created. A `String` takes that to the extreme: the moment `"alice"` exists on the heap, those five characters are frozen for the entire lifetime of that object. You cannot edit them from outside, and `String`'s own methods never edit them either.

Why does this exist? `String` is the single most-used type in any Java program — it shows up as `HashMap` keys, as the class names the class loader resolves, as file paths, SQL text, and values handed between threads. The designers made it immutable so all of that sharing is safe by default. If one piece of code could mutate a `String` that another piece was relying on, every one of those uses would become a latent bug.

Three things in the `String` source enforce the guarantee:

- The characters live in a `private final byte[] value` (it was a `char[]` before Java 9). `final` means the reference can never be repointed; `private` means no outside code can reach the array.
- No method ever writes into that array. `toUpperCase()`, `concat()`, and `replace()` each build and return a **brand-new** `String`.
- The `String` class itself is `final`, so nobody can subclass it and override a method to slip mutation back in.

This is why every "change" is really a fresh allocation. `name = name.toUpperCase()` does not touch `"alice"`; it creates `"ALICE"` and moves the variable, leaving the old object unreachable until garbage collection. The same property is what lets the JVM keep a **String pool**: one `"hello"` literal can be handed to every variable that asks for it, because none of them can corrupt it for the others.

> The variable can be reassigned; the `String` object it used to point at never changes.

That distinction is exactly what an interviewer is listening for. Saying "a `String` can't be changed" is loose — the reference in your variable changes all the time. What can never change is the object behind it, and that single fact is what buys you thread safety, pool sharing, stable hash codes, and security.

sections.title: What Really Happens When You 'Modify' a String
sections.content:
Every 'modification' method allocates a new object and leaves the original untouched. ```mermaid flowchart LR V1["variable name"] -->|"originally points to"| S1["alice @ 0xA100
heap — never changes"] V1 -->|"name = name.toUpperCase()"| V2["variable name
after reassignment"] V2 -->|"now points to"| S2["ALICE @ 0xB200
brand-new object"] S1 -.->|"old object orphaned"| GC["awaits garbage collection"] ``` The variable `name` moved. The `String` `"alice"` did not.

sections.title: Proving Immutability — References and Identity
Benefits of String Immutability
sections.content:
| Benefit | How immutability enables it |
|---|---|
| **Thread safety** | Multiple threads can read the same String object simultaneously — no lock needed because nobody can change it |
| **String pool** | JVM can share one `"hello"` object across all variables that hold it — safe because nobody can mutate it |
| **HashMap key safety** | `hashCode()` never changes — once a String is used as a Map key, it will always hash to the same bucket |
| **Security** | Class names, passwords, file paths passed around can't be tampered with by malicious code after the security check |
| **Caching** | `hashCode()` is computed once and cached inside the object — cheap repeated lookups |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying "a `String` variable can't be changed"** — the variable gets reassigned all the time; it's the *object* that's frozen. Stating it loosely signals you memorized a line rather than understood the mechanism.
- **Thinking methods like `replace()` edit the string in place** — they return a new `String`. Calling `s.replace('a','b')` and ignoring the return value leaves `s` unchanged, so the "fix" silently does nothing.
- **Confusing `final` with immutable** — `final String s` only stops `s` from being reassigned; it says nothing about the object's contents. Immutability comes from `String`'s internals, not your `final` keyword (a `final` field of a mutable type is still mutable).
- **Assuming immutability makes every use thread-safe** — sharing one `String` object is safe, but a non-`final` field you keep reassigning still needs `volatile` or a lock for cross-thread visibility.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`private final byte[] value`** — the backing array is `final` (reference can't be repointed) and `private` (no caller can reach it); since Java 9 it's a `byte[]` plus a coder flag, not `char[]`, halving memory for Latin-1 text.
- **The `String` class is `final`** — you can't subclass it to override methods or inject a mutator, which makes immutability tamper-proof rather than a convention you trust.
- **`hashCode()` is computed once and cached** — the value is stored in a field on first call; that only works because the content can never change, and it's why `String` keys keep `HashMap` lookups cheap.
- **Variable reassignment is not mutation** — `s = s.toUpperCase()` repoints the reference and leaves the original object on the heap until GC; blurring this is the single most common slip.
- **The String pool depends entirely on immutability** — equal literals are deduped to one shared object; if any holder could mutate it, sharing would corrupt every other holder.
- **Immutability of the object ≠ thread safety of a reference** — the `String` is safe to share unlocked, but a field you keep reassigning across threads still needs `volatile` for visibility.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
People say a `String` "can't be changed," but the precise version is what earns the point: the variable holding a `String` gets reassigned constantly — what never changes is **the object it points at**. When you write `name = name.toUpperCase()`, the original `"alice"` is still sitting on the heap exactly as it was; `toUpperCase()` built a new `"ALICE"` and your variable simply moved to it.

Java enforces this with **three things**, not one. The characters live in a `private final` array, so no outside code can reach them and the reference can't be repointed. None of `String`'s methods ever write into that array — `concat()`, `replace()`, and `substring()` all return new objects. And the class itself is `final`, so nobody can subclass it to slip in a mutator. Together that makes immutability **tamper-proof**, not a polite convention.

The reason it matters is everything Java leans on it for. Threads can share a `String` with zero synchronization because there's nothing to race on. The JVM keeps one copy of a literal in the **String pool** and hands it out everywhere. A `String` works as a reliable `HashMap` key because its `hashCode()` is cached once and can never drift. And security-sensitive values like class names or file paths can't be swapped between a check and their use. If I give one line: immutability is what makes `String` safe to share without thinking about it.

questions.question: If String is immutable, why is String concatenation in a loop slow in Java?
questions.title: Why String Concatenation in a Loop Is Slow
questions.direct_answer: Because every `+` on a String creates a new object on the heap and discards the old one. In a loop of N iterations, you create N intermediate String objects — most are immediately garbage. The fix is `StringBuilder`, which maintains a single resizable internal buffer and only creates one String at the end.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the performance consequence of String immutability and know to use StringBuilder in loops.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using String + in a loop without thinking about it — produces O(n²) memory and time cost because each concatenation copies all previous characters into a new object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Java's compiler is smart enough to convert a single-line `s = 'a' + 'b' + 'c'` into a StringBuilder internally — but it cannot do this across loop iterations. The loop case genuinely creates N objects.

sections.title: Why an Innocent `+` Turns into O(n²) Inside a Loop
sections.content:
Joining two strings with `+` produces a **third** `String` that holds the characters of both. That sounds harmless, and for a single `+` it is. The cost only shows up when you do it again and again inside a loop.

Because a `String` is immutable, `result = result + word` can't append `word` onto the end of `result` — the existing object is frozen. So the `+` has to allocate a new `String` big enough for both, copy every character of the old `result` into it, copy `word` after that, and then point `result` at the new object. The old one is left orphaned for the garbage collector.

One `+` is cheap. A loop is where it compounds. On iteration `k`, the running result already holds `k` words, and **all of those characters get copied again** into the next object. Across `N` iterations you copy roughly `1 + 2 + 3 + ... + N` characters — about `N²/2`. That's **O(n²)** in time and memory, and it produces `N` throwaway `String` objects that all become garbage. At a few hundred iterations it's already measurably slow; at tens of thousands it falls off a cliff.

`StringBuilder` exists for exactly this. It holds a single, resizable `char[]` buffer; `append()` writes into the end of that buffer with no new object and no recopying of what's already there. When you're done, one `toString()` produces exactly one `String`. That turns the whole loop from **O(n²)** into **O(n)**.

> `javac` rewrites `"a" + b + "c"` into a single `StringBuilder` — but it cannot do that across loop iterations.

This is the detail that trips people up. A flat, single-statement concatenation is already optimized for you, so `+` there is perfectly fine. Inside a loop the compiler can't know how many times the body runs, so it emits a fresh concatenation per pass and the N-object cost is real. The fix is simply to hoist one `StringBuilder` outside the loop and `append()` inside it.

sections.title: String + in a Loop — N Objects Created
sections.content:
Each box below is a new heap allocation; all but the last are immediately orphaned. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["result = empty string"] --> B["result + words[0]
new String object #1"] B --> C["result + words[1]
new String object #2
copies #1 then appends"] C --> D["result + words[2]
new String object #3
copies #2 then appends"] D --> E["... after N iterations
N objects, all but the last are garbage"] ``` The copying at each step is what makes the total work grow like `N²/2`, not `N`.

sections.title: String + in Loop vs StringBuilder — Same Result, Very Different Cost
String + vs StringBuilder in a Loop
sections.content:
| | `String +` in loop | `StringBuilder.append()` |
|---|---|---|
| New objects per iteration | 1 (plus old one abandoned) | 0 |
| Total memory copies | O(n²) — each step copies all previous chars | O(n) — each char written once |
| Thread safe? | Yes (immutable) | No (use StringBuffer if needed) |
| Readable for single-line | Yes | Slightly more verbose |
| Right choice for loops | No | Yes |
| Compiler optimises? | Only for single-statement chains | N/A — already optimal |

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reaching for `String +` in a loop out of habit** — it reads cleanly but is quietly O(n²); the slowdown is invisible with 10 items and brutal with 10,000, so it sails through tests and bites in production.
- **Assuming "the compiler optimizes it anyway"** — `javac` only collapses a *single statement* into one `StringBuilder`; a loop emits a fresh concatenation each pass, so the N-object cost is genuinely there.
- **Creating a new `StringBuilder` inside the loop** — that defeats the purpose. Allocate one builder before the loop and `append()` into it; otherwise you're back to per-iteration allocation.
- **Using `StringBuffer` "to be safe"** — its method-level locking adds overhead you almost never need. `StringBuilder` is the default; `StringBuffer` only earns its place when one builder is genuinely shared across threads.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Loop `+` is O(n²), not O(n)** — iteration `k` recopies all `k` characters already accumulated, so `N` iterations copy ~`N²/2` chars and create `N` throwaway objects.
- **`StringBuilder` is O(n)** — one resizable `char[]` buffer, `append()` writes in place, a single `toString()` at the end; hoist the builder *outside* the loop.
- **Single-statement `+` is already optimal** — `javac` compiles `"a" + b + "c"` to one `StringBuilder` (via `invokedynamic` + `StringConcatFactory` since Java 9), so `+` outside a loop needs no fixing.
- **The compiler can't optimize across iterations** — it has no way to know the loop body runs more than once, so each pass gets its own concatenation; the N-object cost is genuine.
- **Pre-size the buffer when you know the length** — `new StringBuilder(expectedLen)` avoids internal array doublings (the buffer grows ~2x each time it fills), saving repeated copies.
- **`StringBuffer` is the synchronized twin** — same API, every method locked; choose `StringBuilder` unless one builder is genuinely shared across threads, which is rare.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The thing to get right is that **immutability** turns an innocent-looking `+` into real work. Since the existing `String` can't be appended to, `result = result + word` has to allocate a new object, copy every character of the old `result` into it, copy the new word after that, and throw the old object away. Do it once and nobody notices. Do it `N` times in a loop and each pass recopies everything accumulated so far — so you've copied on the order of `N²/2` characters and created `N` pieces of garbage. That's **O(n²)**, and it's slow well before the numbers look scary.

`StringBuilder` fixes it because it keeps **one resizable buffer** and just writes to the end. `append()` adds the new characters without recopying the old ones, and a single `toString()` at the end gives you one `String`. That's linear instead of quadratic.

The nuance worth mentioning is that **a single-statement** `"a" + b + "c"` is completely fine — the compiler already rewrites it into one `StringBuilder` for you. What it can't do is reach across loop iterations, because it has no idea how many times the body runs. So my rule is simple: `+` for one-off concatenation, and the moment I'm building a string piece by piece, a `StringBuilder` hoisted outside the loop.
